parts.title: Booking a pottery course
parts.context: A man phones a pottery studio to book a course.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a pottery studio to book a course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Good afternoon, Clayworks Studio. Jess speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Hi. I'd like to book a place on one of your pottery courses, please. I've never done any pottery before.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Lovely. In that case you'll want our beginners' course, which is all about learning to use the wheel.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The man has never done pottery before, so 'beginners' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Let me take a few details first. Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Yes, it's Daniel Okafor.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: And could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Sure. O-K-A-F-O-R.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Thanks, Daniel. Now, the beginners' course runs on two different evenings. There's a Monday group and a Tuesday group, both from seven till nine.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Monday would suit me best, actually.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: I'm afraid the Monday group is completely full now. But there are still a few places on Tuesday.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Oh well. Tuesday is fine, I can make that work.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Great. The next Tuesday course was supposed to start on the seventh of October, but our tutor is away that week, so the first session will now be on the fourteenth.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: The fourteenth. OK, I'll put that in my diary. And how long does the course last?

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Most of our courses are six weeks, but the beginners' one is a bit longer, because it takes a while to get the hang of the wheel. It's eight weeks altogether.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Right. And what does the price cover? I saw on your website that it's a hundred and sixty pounds.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: That's right. It covers all your clay, and also the firing, which is when we bake your pieces in the kiln. The only thing that's extra is glaze, if you want your pots to be coloured. There's a small charge for each piece.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Is there anything I need to bring with me?

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Not much. Clay is very messy, so you'll need an apron. If you haven't got one, an old shirt will do.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: OK. Do I need my own tools?

script.speaker: jess
script.text: No, we provide all the tools. But it's a good idea to bring a small box, so you can take your finished pieces home safely. Plastic bags aren't really good enough, and things get broken.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: That makes sense. And is there anywhere to park? I'll be coming straight from work.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: The street outside has double yellow lines, so please don't park there. There's a car park behind the library, just round the corner, and it's free after six.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Perfect. Oh, one more thing. Do you offer any discounts? I'm training to be a nurse, so I'm still a student.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: We do. We don't have a special rate for health workers, but students get ten per cent off. You'll just need to show your student card at the first session.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: Brilliant. So how do I pay?

script.speaker: jess
script.text: We ask for a deposit to hold your place. It's normally fifty pounds, but with the student discount it comes down to forty. You pay the rest at the first session.

script.speaker: daniel
script.text: OK. I'll pay the forty pounds now by card, then.

script.speaker: jess
script.text: Lovely. Let me just get the card machine.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A community garden
parts.context: The manager of a community garden welcomes new volunteers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a community garden talking to a group of new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside Community Garden. I'm Peter Hale, and I manage the garden with a team of about forty volunteers. Before you start work, I'd like to show you how the garden is laid out, so have a look at the map I've given you.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: We're standing just inside the main entrance, at the bottom of the map. As you come through the gate, the first thing on your left is the tool shed. It used to be over by the greenhouse, but we moved it here last year, so that nobody has to carry heavy tools all the way across the garden.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Walk up the main path and, before you reach the crossroads, you'll see the children's garden on your left. Local schools visit every week, and each class has its own little bed there.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: When you get to the crossroads, turn left and keep going right to the end of that path, past the pond. That's where you'll find the compost bins. We used to have them at the other end, on the east side, but the neighbours there complained about the smell, so we moved them as far from the houses as we could.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: If you go straight on at the crossroads instead, the first thing on your right is the herb garden, just in front of the orchard. Feel free to pick a few leaves for your tea at break time. That's what it's there for.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: And right at the top of the main path, where it meets the fence, are our bee hives. Please don't go any closer than the sign, and if you're allergic to stings, do tell me today.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Now, a few practical things. First, watering. People often think the evening is the best time to water, but here it just encourages slugs, so please water before eleven in the morning. The beds by the pond might look damp, but the soil there is sandy and dries out faster than anywhere else. And we try not to use the mains tap at all: everything comes from the rain barrels along the fence, which are hardly ever empty.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Second, please always sign the book in the shed when you arrive. It's not about keeping an eye on you, and our insurance covers you whether you sign in or not. The reason is that our grant from the council depends on showing how many volunteer hours we put in each year, so every hour counts.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Some of you have asked what happens to everything we grow. We don't have a shop or a café, so nothing is sold. Volunteers can take a small bag of whatever is spare at the end of a session, but most of it, around three quarters of the harvest, goes to the food bank in the town centre.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: This month, the priority for new volunteers is the raised beds. The wooden sides on several of them have rotted, and we need to replace them before spring planting. The paths need weeding too, but the Saturday group is doing that, and the new fruit trees won't arrive until November.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Finally, rain. A bit of drizzle doesn't stop us. But if there's heavy rain, please don't just go home. The greenhouse is far too full of seedlings to work in, so we all squeeze into the shed and sort seeds for next year. It's surprisingly sociable.

script.speaker: peter
script.text: Right. Any questions before we start?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Marketing a museum
parts.context: Two business students discuss a marketing project for a local museum with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Maya and Omar, discussing their marketing project for a local museum with their tutor, Dr Clarke. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, how is the museum project going?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Pretty well, I think. We've chosen the Harbour Museum, in the old customs house.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Because it's so close to the university, I suppose?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: People keep saying that, but it wasn't really the reason. Omar's cousin volunteers there, which helped us get permission, but the main reason was that visitor numbers have dropped by about a third in five years. We wanted a real problem to solve.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Good. And have you looked at their visitor survey?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: Yes. We expected it to show that most visitors were tourists, but they're only about a quarter. And price isn't an issue, because entry's free. What really stood out was that hardly anyone under thirty visits. It's almost all families with young children and retired people.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: That's a useful finding. Now, I've read your draft report. The data section is excellent, and the length is about right. What's missing is a clear set of recommendations at the end. At the moment, the reader has to work them out from the data.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: OK, we can fix that. We've also looked at their website, and that's a real problem.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: In what way?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: The information is fine, the opening times are right and so on, and it looks good on a laptop. But on a phone the menu disappears completely, so you can't get to any of the pages. And that's how most young people would find it.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: And what's your next step?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: We wanted to interview the director, but she's away until the end of the month. So next week we're going to run a focus group with eight students who've never been to the museum, to find out what would get them through the door.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Let's talk about the ideas in your plan. You suggested posters on buses.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: We did, but when we got the prices, a month of bus adverts would cost more than the museum's whole marketing budget for the year. So we've dropped that one.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Fair enough. What about the podcast?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: We still like it, but we don't know if anyone would listen. So we're going to make one pilot episode and see how many downloads it gets before we suggest a whole series.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Sensible. And school visits?

script.speaker: omar
script.text: That's the easiest one. The museum already has an education room that's hardly used, and two local teachers have said they're interested. So the museum could start straight away.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Discount vouchers for the café?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: We looked into that, but the café is run by an outside company, so the museum can't offer discounts there. We've taken it out of the plan.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: And finally, the online quiz about the town's history.

script.speaker: omar
script.text: We think it could work on social media, but it might be too long. So we'll try it out with a small group of the museum's followers first, and shorten it if people give up halfway.

script.speaker: clarke
script.text: Good. Send me the revised report by Friday.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the story of glass
parts.context: A lecture on the history of glass and how it is made.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of glass. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at a material we take completely for granted: glass. It's in our windows, our phones and our kitchens, but its history goes back thousands of years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Long before people learned to make glass, they used a natural glass called obsidian, which forms when lava from a volcano cools very quickly. Obsidian breaks with extremely sharp edges, so it was ideal for making blades, and some surgeons still use obsidian scalpels today.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first glass made by people appeared about four and a half thousand years ago, probably in Mesopotamia. It was difficult to make and very expensive, so it wasn't used for anything practical at first. The earliest glass objects we've found are beads, worn as jewellery by the wealthy, and they were often traded as if they were precious stones.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The real turning point came around two thousand years ago, when craftsmen in Syria discovered that they could blow air into molten glass through a hollow pipe. Glassblowing was much faster than the older methods, and suddenly glass became cheap enough for everyday containers, like bottles and jars for oil and wine.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The Romans spread glassblowing across their empire, and they were also the first to put glass in windows. However, it was thick and cloudy, and it was mainly found in public baths, where it kept the heat in while still letting in some light. Most private houses had to wait more than a thousand years for glass windows.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In medieval Europe, glass took on a new role in the great cathedrals. Most people at that time couldn't read, so the coloured windows were used to tell stories from religious texts in pictures. Making them was slow and skilled work, and a single large window could take years to complete.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For centuries, making flat glass for windows remained a problem. Glassmakers had to blow a large bubble or cylinder and then flatten it, which left the glass uneven. The breakthrough came in the nineteen fifties with the float glass process. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin, and because the tin is perfectly flat, the glass spreads out into a perfectly flat sheet. This meant that the glass no longer needed polishing, which had been the slowest and most expensive part of the process. Almost all window glass is still made this way.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Glass has also become central to modern communication. Fibre-optic cables, made from extremely pure glass, carry data as pulses of light under the oceans and across continents. Without them, the internet as we know it simply wouldn't exist.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, researchers are now developing new kinds of glass with remarkable properties. Some can change colour to block sunlight, and one team in Japan has produced a glass that will actually repair itself: if it cracks, the broken surfaces will join together again when pressed. In the next lecture, we'll look at how glass is recycled.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
